questions.q: 'He has ___ friends, so he is always lonely.' few or a few?
questions.a: 'few' — the loneliness clue signals the negative reading (almost none). A wrong answer 'a few' reveals the student reads few/a few as interchangeable spellings — missing the entire attitudinal payload the 'a' carries.
'fewer students' — students are countable. A wrong answer accepting 'less' shows the student doesn't partition English nouns into count/mass — the prerequisite for half the determiner system.

questions.q: '___ knowledge he had saved him.' the few / a little / the little?
questions.a: 'the little' — the small amount of knowledge that existed was sufficient; 'the little' = all of a scarce supply. A wrong answer 'a little' misses that 'the' + little/few collects the whole scarce set — a distinction boards test precisely because it looks trivial.

questions.q: ______ governs the family: few/fewer/many for countables, little/less/much for uncountables, and 'the few/the little' means 'the small amount that exists'.
Fill in the blank: ______ encode attitude: 'few' = almost none (negative), 'a few' = some (positive); 'little' = almost none, 'a little' = some.
Fill in the blank: Two glasses on the desk: 'There is little water' — bad news, nearly empty. 'There is a little water' — good news, ______ for a sip.
What is Quantifiers encode attitude? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Quantifiers encode attitude: 'few' = almost none (negative), 'a few' = some (positive); 'little' = almost none, 'a little' = some.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Quantifiers encode attitude?
questions.a: Students think few/a few differ only in style, not attitude — missing that 'few' is pessimistic.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student selects few/a few/little/a little by intended attitude and countability, uses fewer/less correctly, and distinguishes 'the few' (all of the scarce group) from 'a few'.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Two ______ on the desk: 'There is little water' — bad news, nearly empty. 'There is a little water' — good news, enough for a sip.
